claim: C. elegans fed OP50 and CS180 developed through four larval stages at about the same rate.
source: Wild-type C. elegans fed two different E. coli strains, OP50 and CS180, developed through four larval stages (L1 to L4; Figure 1A) at about the same rate (Figure 1B), before they molted into young adults.
evidence: Supported by Figure 1B showing stage distributions and statistical analysis (p=0.72)

claim: C. elegans grown on CS180 produced fewer progeny compared to animals grown on OP50.
source: However, C. elegans grown on CS180 produced fewer progeny when compared to animals grown on OP50 (Figure 1C, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and source data 1

claim: CS180-fed animals exhibited faster fertilization rates during the first 24 hr of adulthood.
source: In fact, CS180-fed animals exhibited faster fertilization rates during the first 24 hr of adulthood (Figure 1D, Figure 1—source data 1), which is opposite of what would be expected for food level-restricted animals (Maier et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 1D and source data 1, with citation to prior work

claim: Animals fed CS180 had fewer sperm than animals on OP50.
source: Consistent with this idea, animals fed CS180 not only had fewer progeny (Figure 1C, Figure 1—source data 1), but also fewer sperm than animals on OP50 (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E

claim: A significant fraction of worms on CS180 began to express the oogenesis marker lin-41::GFP at the mid-L4 stage, before the marker was observed in any worms on OP50.
source: We found that a significant fraction of worms on CS180 began to express the oogenesis marker lin-41::GFP at the mid-L4 stage, which was before the marker was observed in any worms on OP50 (Figure 1H, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 1H and source data 1

claim: Worms fed CS180 started to express oma-1::GFP at mid-L4 before any OP50-fed worms.
source: Similar to what we observed with lin-41::GFP, worms fed CS180 started to express oma-1::GFP at mid-L4 (20%), again before any OP50-fed worms (Figure 1I, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 1I and source data 1

claim: The gonads of CS180-fed animals had more arrested oocytes than the gonads of age-matched adults on OP50.
source: The gonads of CS180-fed animals also had more arrested oocytes than the gonads of age-matched adults on OP50 (Figure 1J).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1J

claim: The total number of sperm made before the gametogenesis switch to oogenesis can limit the number of progeny in C. elegans.
source: In C. elegans, the total number of sperm made before the gametogenesis switch to oogenesis can limit the number of progeny (Ward and Carrel, 1979).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ward and Carrel, 1979

claim: The rate of oocyte maturation determines the rate of fertilization in C. elegans hermaphrodites.
source: Thus, in C. elegans hermaphrodites, the rate of oocyte maturation determines the rate of fertilization (McCarter et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to McCarter et al., 1999

claim: Worms on CS2429 displayed a lower number of progeny similar to CS180.
source: Interestingly, like on CS180, worms on CS2429 still displayed a lower number of progeny (Figure 2B, Figure 2—source data 1), early oogenesis (Figure 2C, Figure 2—source data 1), and faster fertilization (Figure 2D, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 2B and source data 1

claim: The difference in LPS structure between OP50 and CS180 is insufficient to affect oocyte development.
source: This indicates that this difference in LPS structure is insufficient to affect oocyte development.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that CS2429 (truncated LPS) shows same phenotype as CS180

claim: HT115-fed worms did not exhibit an early oogenesis onset.
source: While worms on the E. coli K-12 HT115 bacteria (Takiff et al., 1989; Dasgupta et al., 1998) produced a similar number of progeny as worms fed CS180 (Figure 2—source data 1), HT115-fed worms did not exhibit an early oogenesis onset (Figure 2E, Figure 2—source data 1) or faster fertilization rates (Figure 2F, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 2E and source data 1

claim: Animals supplemented with CS180-conditioned media showed early expression of the oogenesis marker at mid-L4 and had faster fertilization rates.
source: We found that these animals showed early expression of the oogenesis marker at mid-L4 and had faster fertilization rates, which are unlike the unsupplemented OP50-fed controls (Figure 2G and H, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 2G and H and source data 1

claim: Filtration of CS180-conditioned media through a 0.45 μm nylon membrane removed the cue(s) that promote early oocyte development and fast fertilization.
source: However, filtration of the CS180-conditioned media through a nylon membrane, which has a 0.45 μm diameter pore size, removed the cue(s) that promote early oocyte development and fast fertilization (Figure 2G and H, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 2G and H and source data 1

claim: The CS180-derived cue(s) that modulate oocyte physiology are unlikely to be small molecules, such as free metabolites.
source: Because the cue(s) were lost by filtration through the nylon membrane filters (Hasegawa et al., 2003), the CS180-derived cue(s) that modulate oocyte physiology are unlikely to be small molecules, such as free metabolites.
evidence: Inferred from filtration experiment results, with citation to Hasegawa et al., 2003

claim: The absence of early oogenesis onset on S. marcescens suggests that the CS180 responses are not general innate immune responses.
source: The absence of early oogenesis onset on S. marcescens (Figure 2I, Figure 2—source data 1) suggests that the CS180 responses are not general innate immune responses.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing no early oogenesis on S. marcescens

claim: Bacterial pathogenicity is insufficient to promote earlier oocyte development.
source: Our findings also show that bacterial pathogenicity is insufficient to promote earlier oocyte development.
evidence: Inferred from S. marcescens experiments showing no early oogenesis

claim: Food type can only modulate onset of oogenesis before late L3.
source: Thus, food type can only modulate onset of oogenesis before late L3, consistent with a prior study that showed that germ cell fate determination occurs during this stage (Barton and Kimble, 1990).
evidence: Supported by food-switch experiments and citation to Barton and Kimble, 1990

claim: The critical window for the food-type effect on fertilization rate is after the early part of the fourth larval stage (L4).
source: However, the critical window for the food-type effect on fertilization rate is after the early part of the fourth larval stage (L4; Figure 3C to F, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by food-switch experiments shown in Figure 3C-F and source data 1

claim: The osm-3 mutant produced the same number of offspring on both OP50 and CS180.
source: Accordingly, we tested mutants that impaired different subsets of sensory neurons. Unlike wild type, the osm-3 mutant, which has many defective sensory neurons (Tabish et al., 1995; Taylor et al., 2021), produced the same number of offspring on both OP50 and CS180 (Figure 4A, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 4A and source data 1, with citations

claim: A mutation in odr-1 produced the same number of progeny on OP50 and CS180.
source: Similar to osm-3 mutants, a mutation in the guanylyl cyclase gene odr-1, which impairs a different subset of sensory neurons (L'Etoile and Bargmann, 2000; Taylor et al., 2021), also produced the same number of progeny on OP50 and CS180 (Figure 4A, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 4A and source data 1, with citations

claim: A defect in odr-7, which causes the specific loss of the olfactory neuron AWA, led to more progeny on OP50 than on CS180.
source: However, unlike osm-3 and odr-1 mutants, but like wild type, a defect in the transcription factor gene odr-7, which causes the specific loss of the olfactory neuron AWA (Sengupta et al., 1994), led to more progeny on OP50 than on CS180 (Figure 4A, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 4A and source data 1, with citation

claim: Loss of the ASJ neurons suppressed the differences in progeny number on OP50 versus CS180.
source: Interestingly, loss of the ASJ neurons suppressed the differences in progeny number (Figure 4A, Figure 4—source data 1) on OP50 versus CS180.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 4A and source data 1

claim: The neuron ASJ modulates the worm's total progeny in response to food cues.
source: Thus, our data show that, unlike ASI, ASK, and AWA, the neuron ASJ modulates the worm's total progeny in response to food cues.
evidence: Inferred from ASJ ablation experiments showing loss of food-type differences

claim: Reduction-of-function mutations in daf-2 reduced or abolished the food-type differences in total progeny.
source: Reduction-of-function mutations in daf-2, the C. elegans insulin-like growth factor receptor (Kimura et al., 1997; Gems et al., 1998), reduced or abolished the food-type differences in total progeny (Figure 4B, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 4B and source data 1, with citations

claim: A loss-of-function mutation in daf-16 still led to food-type differences in the number of progeny on OP50 and CS180.
source: In contrast, a loss-of-function mutation in daf-16, the FOXO-like transcription factor that is antagonized by DAF-2 (Lin et al., 1997; Ogg et al., 1997), still led to food-type differences in the number of progeny on OP50 and CS180 (Figure 4B and E, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 4B and E and source data 1, with citations

claim: Deletion of either ins-1 or daf-28 did not alter the OP50- or CS180-dependent progeny number.
source: Deletion of either ins-1 or daf-28 did not alter the OP50- or CS180-dependent progeny number (Figure 4C, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 4C and source data 1

claim: ins-6 deletion mutants lost the food-type differences in total progeny.
source: However, ins-6 deletion mutants lost the food-type differences in total progeny (Figure 4D and E, Figure 4—source data 1), which were restored when daf-16 was also deleted (Figure 4E, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 4D and E and source data 1

claim: osm-3 mutants failed to exhibit early oogenesis on CS180 during mid-L4.
source: Similar to the loss of food-type differences in its total progeny (Figure 4A, Figure 4—source data 1), osm-3 mutants failed to exhibit early oogenesis on CS180 during mid-L4 (Figure 5A, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 5A and source data 1

claim: ASJ-ablated worms showed no early expression of the oogenesis marker lin-41::GFP at mid-L4.
source: More importantly, ASJ-ablated worms showed no early expression of the oogenesis marker lin-41::GFP at mid-L4 and decreased lin-41::GFP even during late L4 and lethargus (Figure 5A, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 5A and source data 1

claim: ASJ neurons play a major role in promoting early oogenesis.
source: These findings demonstrate that ASJ neurons not only modulate the animal's number of progeny, but also play a major role in promoting early oogenesis.
evidence: Inferred from ASJ ablation experiments showing delayed oogenesis

claim: Both daf-2 reduction-of-function mutants lost the early expression of the oogenesis marker lin-41::GFP on CS180.
source: Indeed, both daf-2 reduction-of-function mutants lost the early expression of the oogenesis marker lin-41::GFP on CS180 (Figure 5B, Figure 5—source data 1), whereas daf-16 deletion mutants continued to have early oogenesis on CS180 (Figure 5C, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 5B and source data 1

claim: daf-16 deletion mutants continued to have early oogenesis on CS180.
source: Indeed, both daf-2 reduction-of-function mutants lost the early expression of the oogenesis marker lin-41::GFP on CS180 (Figure 5B, Figure 5—source data 1), whereas daf-16 deletion mutants continued to have early oogenesis on CS180 (Figure 5C, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 5C and source data 1

claim: ins-6 mutants had no early expression of lin-41::GFP at mid-L4 on CS180.
source: However, ins-6 mutants had no early expression of lin-41::GFP (Figure 5D and F, Figure 5—source data 1) or oma-1::GFP (Figure 5E, Figure 5—source data 1) at mid-L4 on CS180.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 5D and F and source data 1

claim: Of the three ILPs tested, ins-6 alone is sufficient to modulate the food type-dependent onset of oogenesis.
source: Thus, our data show that of the three ILPs tested, ins-6 alone is sufficient to modulate the food type-dependent onset of oogenesis (Figures 5 and 6).
evidence: Inferred from comparison of ins-1, daf-28, and ins-6 mutant phenotypes

claim: The lack of early oogenesis at mid-L4 in ins-6 mutants cannot be rescued by the loss of daf-16.
source: Surprisingly, however, the lack of early oogenesis at mid-L4 in ins-6 mutants cannot be rescued by the loss of daf-16 (Figure 5F, Figure 5—source data 1), which suggests that ins-6 modulates early oogenesis independent of daf-16.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 5F and source data 1

claim: ins-6 modulates early oogenesis independent of daf-16.
source: Surprisingly, however, the lack of early oogenesis at mid-L4 in ins-6 mutants cannot be rescued by the loss of daf-16 (Figure 5F, Figure 5—source data 1), which suggests that ins-6 modulates early oogenesis independent of daf-16.
evidence: Inferred from epistasis analysis showing daf-16 deletion does not rescue ins-6 phenotype

claim: Worms grown on CS180 showed higher ins-6p::mCherry expression in ASJ, but not in ASI, at mid-to-late L3.
source: At mid-to-late L3, the critical period when the food source modulates oogenesis onset (Figure 3B, Figure 3—source data 1), worms grown on CS180 showed higher ins-6p::mCherry expression in ASJ, but not in ASI, unlike worms on OP50 (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 6A

claim: ASJ-expressed ins-6, but not ASI-expressed ins-6, is sufficient to rescue the oogenesis onset phenotype of ins-6 mutants.
source: We also found that ASJ-expressed ins-6, but not ASI-expressed ins-6, is sufficient to rescue the oogenesis onset phenotype of ins-6 mutants, comparable to the rescue observed when ins-6 expression is driven from its own promoter (Figure 6B, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 6B and source data 1

claim: Loss of ins-6 from ASJ delayed oogenesis, despite the continued presence of ins-6 in ASI.
source: Loss of ins-6 from ASJ delayed oogenesis, despite the continued presence of ins-6 in ASI (Figure 6C, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 6C and source data 1

claim: ASJ-expressed ins-6 is both sufficient and necessary to promote early oogenesis on the CS180 food source.
source: Thus, we show that ASJ-expressed ins-6 is both sufficient and necessary to promote early oogenesis on the CS180 food source.
evidence: Inferred from rescue and cell-specific deletion experiments

claim: A mutation in either osm-3 or odr-3 suppressed the faster fertilization on CS180.
source: While the odr-1 mutation had little effect on food type-dependent fertilization rates (Figure 7—source data 1), a mutation in either osm-3 or another sensory gene, the G protein α subunit odr-3 (Roayaie et al., 1998), suppressed the faster fertilization on CS180 (Figure 7A and B, Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 7A and B and source data 1, with citation

claim: Ablation of either ADF or ASH had no effect on the food type-induced variation in fertilization rates.
source: Ablation of either ADF or ASH had no effect on the food type-induced variation in fertilization rates (Figure 7C and D, Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 7C and D and source data 1

claim: Loss of either ASI or ASK did not abolish the food-type differences in fertilization.
source: While the global fertilization rates were lower on OP50 and CS180, loss of either ASI or ASK again did not abolish the food-type differences in fertilization (Figure 7E and F, Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 7E and F and source data 1

claim: The ASJ neurons did not affect fertilization rates on OP50 versus CS180.
source: In addition, the ASJ neurons, which modulate onset of oogenesis (Figure 5A and E, Figure 5—source data 1), did not affect fertilization rates on OP50 versus CS180 (Figure 7G, Figure 7—source data 1), suggesting that ASJ specifically influences oogenesis, but not fertilization.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 7G and source data 1

claim: ASJ specifically influences oogenesis, but not fertilization.
source: In addition, the ASJ neurons, which modulate onset of oogenesis (Figure 5A and E, Figure 5—source data 1), did not affect fertilization rates on OP50 versus CS180 (Figure 7G, Figure 7—source data 1), suggesting that ASJ specifically influences oogenesis, but not fertilization.
evidence: Inferred from ASJ ablation showing no effect on fertilization but effect on oogenesis

claim: Loss of AWA suppressed the food-type differences in fertilization.
source: While loss of AWB and AWC did not eliminate the fertilization rate differences on OP50 and CS180 (Figure 7H and I, Figure 7—source data 1), loss of AWA (Sengupta et al., 1994; Yoshida et al., 2012) suppressed the food-type differences in fertilization (Figure 7J, Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 7J and source data 1, with citations

claim: AWA-dependent regulation of fertilization is independent of the AWA-specific olfactory receptor ODR-10.
source: However, this AWA-dependent regulation of fertilization is independent of the AWA-specific olfactory receptor ODR-10 (Figure 7—source data 1; Sengupta et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in source data 1, with citation

claim: Absence of AWA had no effect on early onset of oogenesis on CS180.
source: We found that absence of AWA had no effect on early onset of oogenesis on CS180 (Figure 7L, Figure 7—source data 1), similar to its lack of effect on progeny number (Figure 4A, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 7L and source data 1

claim: On given diets, there are specific neurons that influence distinct aspects of oocyte development and physiology: ASJ for early oogenesis versus AWA for fertilization.
source: Thus, on given diets, we show that there are specific neurons that influence distinct aspects of oocyte development and physiology: ASJ for early oogenesis versus AWA for fertilization.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of ASJ and AWA ablation phenotypes

claim: The strong reduction-of-function mutant daf-2(e1370) suppressed global fertilization rates.
source: The weak reduction-of-function mutant daf-2(e1368) or the null daf-16(mu86) mutant had little or no significant effect on fertilization (Figure 8A and C, Figure 8—source data 1), but the stronger reduction-of-function mutant daf-2(e1370) (Lin et al., 1997; Gems et al., 1998) suppressed global fertilization rates (Figure 8B, Figure 8—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 8B and source data 1, with citations

claim: The daf-2(e1370) mutant fertilization rate on OP50 still differed from that on CS180.
source: However, the daf-2(e1370) mutant fertilization rate on OP50 still differed from that on CS180 (Figure 8B, Figure 8—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 8B and source data 1

claim: The DAF-2 receptor modulates overall fertilization rates, but not necessarily in response to food-derived cues.
source: This suggests that the DAF-2 receptor modulates overall fertilization rates, but not necessarily in response to food-derived cues.
evidence: Inferred from daf-2(e1370) showing reduced fertilization but still food-type differences

claim: The AWA food type-dependent influence on fertilization differs from the effects of insulin receptor signaling on this process.
source: For this reason, the AWA food type-dependent influence on fertilization differs from the effects of insulin receptor signaling on this process.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of AWA and daf-2 phenotypes

claim: A single deletion of ins-6, daf-28, or ins-1 had no effect on fertilization rates.
source: A single deletion of any of these ILPs had no effect on fertilization rates (Figure 8D to F, Figure 8—source data 1), and deletion mutant combinations of these ILPs (Figure 8—source data 1) did not exhibit any robust phenotypes that mirrored those of the strong daf-2(e1370) mutant phenotypes.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 8D-F and source data 1

claim: There are multiple ILPs that act through the DAF-2 receptor to regulate fertilization.
source: This implies that there are multiple ILPs that act through the DAF-2 receptor to regulate fertilization.
evidence: Inferred from lack of phenotype in single and combined ILP deletions

claim: The set of ILP activities that regulates fertilization is distinct from the set of ILPs that regulates onset of oogenesis.
source: Notably, our findings indicate that the set of ILP activities that regulates fertilization is distinct from the set of ILPs that regulates onset of oogenesis.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of ILP effects on oogenesis versus fertilization

claim: Distinct sensory neurons acting through insulin-dependent and -independent signaling mechanisms influence specific steps in oocyte development and physiology in response to food-derived cues.
source: Here, we show that distinct sensory neurons acting through insulin-dependent and -independent signaling mechanisms influence specific steps in oocyte development and physiology in response to food-derived cues.
evidence: Summary inference from all experimental results

claim: Discrete aspects of oocyte biology—oocyte fate determination and successful oocyte fertilization—are subject to different sets of cues that are sensed by different cells.
source: Thus, discrete aspects of oocyte biology—oocyte fate determination and successful oocyte fertilization—are subject to different sets of cues that are sensed by different cells that work together to control the production of an animal's total progeny.
evidence: Summary inference from all experimental results

claim: The chemosensory neuron ASJ promotes early onset of oogenesis.
source: Unlike the olfactory neuron AWA, the chemosensory neuron ASJ promotes early onset of oogenesis (Figure 7L, Figure 7—source data 1, Figure 9).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 7L and source data 1, and Figure 9

claim: The ASJ-dependent effect on oogenesis does not appear to be a general response to stress, like pathogen stress.
source: This ASJ-dependent effect does not appear to be a general response to stress, like pathogen stress (Figure 2I, Figure 2—source data 1), but a response to specific food cues that are likely not small metabolites (Figure 2G, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Inferred from S. marcescens and filtration experiments

claim: The olfactory neuron AWA promotes the increased fertilization rates on the CS180 food source.
source: In contrast, the olfactory neuron AWA promotes the increased fertilization rates on the CS180 food source, but not ASJ and the other neurons that we have so far tested (Figure 7C to K, Figure 7—source data 1, Figure 9).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 7C-K and source data 1, and Figure 9

claim: The sensory cue(s) that promote early oogenesis differ from the sensory cue(s) that affect fertilization.
source: Together these data suggest that the sensory cue(s) that promote early oogenesis differ from the sensory cue(s) that affect fertilization.
evidence: Inferred from different neurons (ASJ vs AWA) regulating different processes

claim: AWA is most likely not the only sensory neuron involved in food type-dependent fertilization.
source: While AWA has a major role in food type-dependent fertilization, it is most likely not the only sensory neuron involved in this process.
evidence: Inferred from osm-3 mutation also affecting fertilization

claim: The involvement of multiple sensory neurons would make for a more sensitive and efficient physiology.
source: Thus, the involvement of multiple sensory neurons would make for a more sensitive and efficient physiology.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about the adaptive value of multiple neurons

claim: ASJ might regulate oogenesis onset by regulating the first switch that occurs in the C. elegans germline, mitosis to meiosis.
source: This suggests that this sensory neuron might regulate oogenesis onset by regulating the first switch that occurs in the C. elegans germline, mitosis (i.e., proliferation) to meiosis (i.e., differentiation) (Kimble and Crittenden, 2007).
evidence: Speculative inference from ASJ affecting both proliferation and oogenesis, with citation

claim: Food type can only modulate onset of oogenesis before the late L3 stage, which coincides with the time before germ cells enter meiosis.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, we demonstrate that food type can only modulate onset of oogenesis before the late L3 stage (Figure 3B, Figure 3—source data 1), which coincides with the time before germ cells enter meiosis (Kimble and Crittenden, 2007).
evidence: Supported by food-switch experiments and citation to Kimble and Crittenden, 2007

claim: Specific ILPs regulate discrete stages of oocyte physiology.
source: Here, we find that specific ILPs regulate discrete stages of oocyte physiology.
evidence: Summary inference from ILP experiments

claim: The ILP INS-6 acts from the ASJ neuron to modulate food type-dependent early oogenesis.
source: The ILP INS-6 acts from the ASJ neuron to modulate food type-dependent early oogenesis (Figure 6B and C, Figure 6—source data 1, Figure 9), whereas it appears to have little or no effect on oocyte fertilization rates (Figure 8D, Figure 8—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 6B, C, 8D and source data, and Figure 9

claim: INS-6 appears to have little or no effect on oocyte fertilization rates.
source: The ILP INS-6 acts from the ASJ neuron to modulate food type-dependent early oogenesis (Figure 6B and C, Figure 6—source data 1, Figure 9), whereas it appears to have little or no effect on oocyte fertilization rates (Figure 8D, Figure 8—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 8D and source data 1

claim: DAF-2 regulates overall fertilization independent of food sources.
source: Although insulin receptor DAF-2 signaling does not appear to mediate the AWA neuron-dependent food-type effects on fertilization, DAF-2 does regulate overall fertilization independent of food sources (Figure 8B, Figure 8—source data 1, Figure 9), where its ILP ligands remain to be identified.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 8B and source data 1, and Figure 9

claim: Different ILPs regulate specific stages of oogenesis—onset versus maturation.
source: Since fertilization depends on oocyte maturation (McCarter et al., 1999), our data also suggest that different ILPs regulate specific stages of oogenesis—onset versus maturation.
evidence: Inferred from INS-6 affecting oogenesis onset but not fertilization, with citation

claim: At least one ILP, INS-6, can act independent of DAF-16.
source: Our findings further suggest that at least one of these ILPs, INS-6, can act independent of DAF-16, a known transcriptional effector of the DAF-2 receptor (Figure 5F, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 5F and source data 1

claim: Distinct insulin-like signaling mechanisms—daf-16-independent and daf-16-dependent—might be necessary for optimal oogenesis and fertilization.
source: Distinct insulin-like signaling mechanisms—daf-16-independent and daf-16-dependent—might be necessary for optimal oogenesis and fertilization.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on observed daf-16 independence of ins-6

claim: Distinct ILP signaling mechanisms that can respond to disparate environmental cues might explain the variability in the number of progeny of daf-16 mutants.
source: Hence, distinct ILP signaling mechanisms that can respond to disparate environmental cues might also explain the variability in the number of progeny of daf-16 mutants (Figure 4B and E, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on observed phenotypic variability

claim: ILPs might encode and integrate diverse cues that influence oocyte development.
source: ILPs might encode and integrate diverse cues that influence oocyte development.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on multiple ILPs with different functions

claim: It is possible that the multiple ILPs present in other animals will also have specific roles in coordinating oogenesis with fluctuations in a given environment.
source: Considering the pleiotropic effects of insulin signaling on metazoan reproduction (Das and Arur, 2017), it is possible that the multiple ILPs present in other animals (Allen et al., 2015) will also have specific roles in coordinating oogenesis with fluctuations in a given environment.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on C. elegans findings and citations to reviews

claim: Successful fertilization will require the careful integration of multiple environmental inputs through ILPs acting on the germline from neuronal, and potentially non-neuronal, cells.
source: Thus, our study suggests that successful fertilization will require the careful integration of multiple environmental inputs through ILPs acting on the germline from neuronal, and potentially non-neuronal, cells.
evidence: Summary inference from all experimental results

claim: Sensory neurons influence food-dependent survival in C. elegans.
source: In the worm Caenorhabditis elegans, sensory neurons influence food-dependent survival (Maier et al., 2010) and germline physiology (Dalfó et al., 2012; Sowa et al., 2015; Aprison and Ruvinsky, 2017; Perez et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Maier et al., 2010

claim: Sensory neurons influence germline physiology in C. elegans.
source: In the worm Caenorhabditis elegans, sensory neurons influence food-dependent survival (Maier et al., 2010) and germline physiology (Dalfó et al., 2012; Sowa et al., 2015; Aprison and Ruvinsky, 2017; Perez et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dalfó et al., 2012; Sowa et al., 2015; Aprison and Ruvinsky, 2017; Perez et al., 2021

claim: In the germline of the C. elegans hermaphrodite, germ cells first undergo spermatogenesis, before switching to oogenesis.
source: In the germline of the C. elegans hermaphrodite, germ cells first undergo spermatogenesis, before switching to oogenesis (Figure 1A; reviewed by Kimble and Crittenden, 2007).
evidence: Established knowledge with citation to review by Kimble and Crittenden, 2007

claim: After oogenesis begins, oocytes undergo arrest at the diakinesis stage of prophase I.
source: After oogenesis begins, oocytes undergo arrest at the diakinesis stage of prophase I (reviewed by Greenstein, 2005).
evidence: Established knowledge with citation to review by Greenstein, 2005

claim: Oocytes are released from arrest in an assembly-line manner by a hormone secreted from sperm.
source: Oocytes are released from this arrest in an assembly-line manner by a hormone secreted from sperm, where the oocyte most proximal to the spermatheca matures first (McCarter et al., 1999; Miller et al., 2001).
evidence: Established knowledge with citations to McCarter et al., 1999; Miller et al., 2001

claim: Once released from arrest, the oocyte is immediately ovulated into the spermatheca, where it is fertilized by a sperm.
source: Once released from arrest, the oocyte is also immediately ovulated into the spermatheca, where it is fertilized by a sperm (McCarter et al., 1999; Miller et al., 2001).
evidence: Established knowledge with citations to McCarter et al., 1999; Miller et al., 2001

claim: Some C. elegans sensory neurons modulate germ cell proliferation in response to food or pheromones.
source: Some of the C. elegans sensory neurons have been shown to modulate germ cell proliferation (Dalfó et al., 2012; Aprison and Ruvinsky, 2017) and oocyte senescence (Sowa et al., 2015) in response to food or pheromones.
evidence: Supported by citations to Dalfó et al., 2012; Aprison and Ruvinsky, 2017

claim: Some C. elegans sensory neurons modulate oocyte senescence in response to food or pheromones.
source: Some of the C. elegans sensory neurons have been shown to modulate germ cell proliferation (Dalfó et al., 2012; Aprison and Ruvinsky, 2017) and oocyte senescence (Sowa et al., 2015) in response to food or pheromones.
evidence: Supported by citation to Sowa et al., 2015

claim: Worms have 40 insulin-like peptides (ILPs).
source: Worms have 40 insulin-like peptides (ILPs; Duret et al., 1998; Kawano et al., 2000; Pierce et al., 2001; Li et al., 2003), many of which are expressed in sensory neurons and could act alone or combinatorially to regulate several physiological programs (Cornils et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2013; Ritter et al., 2013; Fernandes de Abreu et al., 2014).
evidence: Established knowledge with citations to Duret et al., 1998; Kawano et al., 2000; Pierce et al., 2001; Li et al., 2003

claim: Many ILPs are expressed in sensory neurons and could act alone or combinatorially to regulate several physiological programs.
source: Worms have 40 insulin-like peptides (ILPs; Duret et al., 1998; Kawano et al., 2000; Pierce et al., 2001; Li et al., 2003), many of which are expressed in sensory neurons and could act alone or combinatorially to regulate several physiological programs (Cornils et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2013; Ritter et al., 2013; Fernandes de Abreu et al., 2014).
evidence: Established knowledge with citations to Cornils et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2013; Ritter et al., 2013; Fernandes de Abreu et al., 2014

claim: Two ILPs, ins-3 and ins-33, regulate germ cell proliferation.
source: Indeed, two ILPs, ins-3 and ins-33, have already been shown to regulate germ cell proliferation (Michaelson et al., 2010); however, the cells that secrete these signals that affect the germline are unknown.
evidence: Supported by citation to Michaelson et al., 2010

claim: The cells that secrete ins-3 and ins-33 that affect the germline are unknown.
source: Indeed, two ILPs, ins-3 and ins-33, have already been shown to regulate germ cell proliferation (Michaelson et al., 2010); however, the cells that secrete these signals that affect the germline are unknown.
evidence: Statement of knowledge gap

claim: The chemosensory neurons ASJ modulate oogenesis onset through the insulin-like peptide (ILP) INS-6.
source: The chemosensory neurons ASJ modulate oogenesis onset through the insulin-like peptide (ILP) INS-6.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings from the study

claim: The olfactory neurons AWA regulate food type-dependent differences in C. elegans fertilization rates, but not onset of oogenesis.
source: In contrast, other sensory neurons, the olfactory neurons AWA, regulate food type-dependent differences in C. elegans fertilization rates, but not onset of oogenesis.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings from the study

claim: AWA modulates fertilization rates at least partly in parallel to insulin receptor signaling.
source: AWA modulates fertilization rates at least partly in parallel to insulin receptor signaling, since the insulin receptor DAF-2 regulates fertilization independently of food type, which requires ILPs other than INS-6.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings from the study

claim: The insulin receptor DAF-2 regulates fertilization independently of food type, which requires ILPs other than INS-6.
source: AWA modulates fertilization rates at least partly in parallel to insulin receptor signaling, since the insulin receptor DAF-2 regulates fertilization independently of food type, which requires ILPs other than INS-6.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings from the study

claim: Optimal reproduction requires the integration of diverse food-derived inputs through multiple neuronal signals acting on the C. elegans germline.
source: Together our findings suggest that optimal reproduction requires the integration of diverse food-derived inputs through multiple neuronal signals acting on the C. elegans germline.
evidence: Summary inference from all experimental findings

claim: OP50 is derived from an E. coli B strain.
source: OP50 is derived from an E. coli B strain (Brenner, 1974); CS180, from an E. coli K-12 strain (Pradel et al., 1992).
evidence: Established knowledge with citation to Brenner, 1974

claim: CS180 is derived from an E. coli K-12 strain.
source: OP50 is derived from an E. coli B strain (Brenner, 1974); CS180, from an E. coli K-12 strain (Pradel et al., 1992).
evidence: Established knowledge with citation to Pradel et al., 1992

claim: One of the differences between OP50 and CS180 bacterial strains is the outer core structures of the lipopolysaccharides (LPS) on their cell walls.
source: One of the differences between the two bacterial strains is the outer core structures of the lipopolysaccharides (LPS) on their cell walls (Maier et al., 2010, and references therein).
evidence: Established knowledge with citation to Maier et al., 2010

claim: The OP50 LPS is shorter than the CS180 LPS.
source: The OP50 LPS is shorter than the CS180 LPS (Figure 2A; Maier et al., 2010).
evidence: Established knowledge with citation to Maier et al., 2010 and shown in Figure 2A

claim: CS2429 is a K-12 strain that is derived from CS180 but has a truncated LPS.
source: To test if this difference in LPS alters oogenesis onset and fertilization rate, we examined wild-type C. elegans oocyte development on E. coli CS2429, which is a K-12 strain that is derived from CS180 but has a truncated LPS (Figure 2A; Pradel et al., 1992; Zhang et al., 2006).
evidence: Established knowledge with citations to Pradel et al., 1992; Zhang et al., 2006

claim: During the larval stages, ins-6 is expressed in two sensory neurons, ASI and ASJ.
source: During the larval stages, ins-6 is expressed in two sensory neurons, ASI and ASJ (Cornils et al., 2011).
evidence: Established knowledge with citation to Cornils et al., 2011

claim: ASJ neurons express at least three potential ILP ligands for the DAF-2 receptor: INS-1, INS-6, and DAF-28.
source: Because ASJ neurons express at least three potential ILP ligands for the DAF-2 receptor, INS-1 (Kodama et al., 2006; Tomioka et al., 2006), INS-6 (Cornils et al., 2011), and DAF-28 (Li et al., 2003; Taylor et al., 2021), we tested the effects of these three peptides on progeny number.
evidence: Established knowledge with citations to Kodama et al., 2006; Tomioka et al., 2006; Cornils et al., 2011; Li et al., 2003; Taylor et al., 2021

claim: Insulin signaling is an important regulator of oogenesis, where impaired signaling leads to reproductive deficits across many species.
source: Insulin signaling is an important regulator of oogenesis, where impaired signaling leads to reproductive deficits across many species (reviewed by Das and Arur, 2017).
evidence: Established knowledge with citation to review by Das and Arur, 2017
